lessons.title: What a task is
lessons.subtitle: And what makes a good one
lessons.body: And what makes a good one Say what a benchmark task is: an environment, a goal and a verdict Explain the three properties a good task set has Describe what a difficulty mix does to a score A task is a starting state, a goal, and something that decides whether the goal was reached. A good task set is diverse, verified, and hard enough that the trivial strategies fail. The difficulty mix is a choice, and it decides what the score means.

lessons.title: The score and its uncertainty
lessons.subtitle: What a number on a task set means
lessons.body: What a number on a task set means Explain why a score on a task set is an estimate rather than a fact Compute the interval on a score, and say why the usual one is wrong near zero Compute how many tasks a given difference needs The tasks are a sample, and the score estimates the rate on the population. The interval on a proportion is not symmetric, and near zero the normal approximation is nonsense. A difference between two systems has to be bigger than the noise before it means anything.

lessons.title: The evaluation criterion
lessons.subtitle: The two conditions
lessons.body: The two conditions State the two conditions a solution must satisfy Say what each condition is for, and what fails without it Explain why the criterion is the hardest part of a benchmark to get right The failing test must start failing and end passing, and the passing tests must keep passing. The first condition alone is satisfied by a solver that changes the test. The second condition is what makes the first one mean something.

lessons.title: The cheat
lessons.subtitle: What a criterion has to catch
lessons.body: What a criterion has to catch Describe the failure mode a solver that changes the test exploits Explain how the criterion catches it Say what a score means when the criterion is weak A solver that can change the test does not have to solve the task. The criterion catches it by requiring the other tests to keep passing, and by distrusting a patch that touches a test. A benchmark whose criterion is weak measures something else, and does not say what.

lessons.title: The agentless baseline
lessons.subtitle: What a score has to beat
lessons.body: What a score has to beat Describe the agentless baseline and what it does Explain why it is the number every agent has to beat Compare it with an agent on the same tasks The baseline retrieves the relevant file and makes one obvious change. Most of what an agent adds is the ability to try again, and that has a price. The comparison has to be on the same tasks, with the same verifier.

lessons.title: The price of trying again
lessons.subtitle: What the agent spends
lessons.body: What the agent spends Measure the number of attempts an agent makes Compare the agent with the baseline on the same tasks Say what the extra attempts buy and what they cost An agent that tries several times solves more tasks and makes more attempts. The attempts are the cost, and they are paid in model calls. So the comparison is not between the two scores but between the two scores per attempt.

lessons.title: One run or many
lessons.subtitle: The variance, and the pass@k estimator
lessons.body: The variance, and the pass@k estimator Compute the variance of a score across runs Explain why a single run overstates pass@k, and what the unbiased estimate is Say how many samples a comparison needs A solver is stochastic, so one run is one sample of a distribution. The naive estimate of pass@k is biased upwards, and the correction is what makes two sample budgets comparable. The paired comparison is more sensitive than comparing two independent scores.

lessons.title: Has the model seen it?
lessons.subtitle: Contamination, and the overlap that finds it
lessons.body: Contamination, and the overlap that finds it Describe what benchmark contamination is and why it invalidates a score Measure it with an n-gram overlap, and report the two rates it gives Say what the length of the n-gram decides, and what the threshold decides A task the model has already seen is not a measurement of anything. The detection is an overlap test, and it has two failure modes: too short a match catches ordinary text, too long a match misses an edited copy. So the length and the threshold are decisions, and the rates they give are the report.

lessons.title: What a crawl gives you
lessons.subtitle: The shape of the raw material
lessons.body: The shape of the raw material Describe the four properties of a web crawl that make it hard to train on Explain why a corpus is measured by the model it produces rather than by its size Read the ablation table of a filtering pipeline as a set of measurements A crawl is large, noisy, duplicated and partly adversarial. The score of a filter is the model trained on what survives it, not the number of documents it removed. Filtering is a benchmark: the same rules, the same budget, the same metric.

lessons.title: The quality–quantity frontier
lessons.subtitle: What a fixed compute budget buys
lessons.body: What a fixed compute budget buys State the trade-off a fixed compute budget forces between data quantity and data quality Explain why a smaller, cleaner dataset can beat a larger, noisier one Compute the effective number of tokens a filtering budget actually buys At a fixed compute budget, the tokens you can afford are the ones that matter. Filtering is a trade: you spend compute on selection to buy back the compute you spend on training. A corpus of a hundred billion tokens is not a hundred billion tokens of training.

lessons.title: The filtering pipeline
lessons.subtitle: The order of the filters is part of the method
lessons.body: The order of the filters is part of the method List the stages of a filtering pipeline in the order they are applied and say why Explain why cheap structural filters run before expensive model-based ones Read a stage-by-stage count and say what it implies about the corpus Structural filters first, model-based filters second, deduplication last. Every filter that runs late has to look at more documents. A filter that removes a document the model would have learned from is a bug, not a filter.

lessons.title: The reference model
lessons.subtitle: Perplexity, and why the model has to be an n-gram model
lessons.body: Perplexity, and why the model has to be an n-gram model Define the perplexity of a document under a language model Explain why a unigram model fails to remove boilerplate and an n-gram model succeeds Compute a document’s perplexity with stupid backoff Perplexity is the exponential of the mean negative log-likelihood per token. Stupid backoff discounts the probability once for every level of context that is missing. Boilerplate has common words in an unusual arrangement, and only the arrangement gives it away.

lessons.title: Exact and fuzzy
lessons.subtitle: Shingles, Jaccard, and a search that is not quadratic
lessons.body: Shingles, Jaccard, and a search that is not quadratic Define the Jaccard similarity of two shingle sets Explain how a MinHash signature estimates it and what its error is Describe how Locality-Sensitive Hashing makes the search sub-quadratic A document is a set of its token n-grams, and two documents are duplicates when those sets overlap. A MinHash signature estimates the Jaccard similarity in k hash functions instead of |A ∩ B| comparisons. The band structure of the LSH index decides which pairs are compared for real.

lessons.title: Decontamination
lessons.subtitle: A benchmark the model has seen is not a measurement
lessons.body: A benchmark the model has seen is not a measurement Explain what decontamination is for and how it differs from deduplication Apply an n-gram overlap test between a corpus and a benchmark State the two ways a decontamination procedure can be wrong Deduplication removes copies of each other; decontamination removes copies of the test set. The overlap test is an n-gram test, and the n has to be long enough to be unmistakable. A decontamination procedure that is too aggressive removes real data; one that is too lax leaves the leak in.

lessons.title: A mixture is a policy
lessons.subtitle: Proportions, domains, and what they cost
lessons.body: Proportions, domains, and what they cost Describe a data mixture as a probability distribution over domains Explain why a mixture is a decision about which capability to buy Measure the per-domain loss of a model trained under a given mixture The mixture decides how much of the model’s capacity goes to each kind of text. A domain that is under-represented is a domain the model will be weak in. The average loss is not the loss that matters when the use is specialised.

lessons.title: Optimising the mixture
lessons.subtitle: The worst domain, and a closed-form answer
lessons.body: The worst domain, and a closed-form answer Explain the group distributionally robust objective and the update it produces Fit a linear model of a domain’s loss as a function of its weight Solve the mixture problem in closed form and check the solution Name the two steps of the method, and what has to hold for the proxy’s weights to travel to a bigger model Group DRO raises the weight of whichever group is doing worst, and trains on the reweighted sample. If each domain’s loss is linear in its weight, the optimal mixture equalises the active domains. The optimal mixture is found by a one-dimensional search for the level at which the weights sum to one. The weights are learned on a proxy and extrapolated for the target, so the proxy’s ranking has to agree with the target’s — where it does not, the handed-over weights are the weights of a different run.

lessons.title: Recursive training
lessons.subtitle: What a model writes, and what a model trained on it keeps
lessons.body: What a model writes, and what a model trained on it keeps Describe the recursive training loop and the model it produces at each generation Explain why the tail of a distribution is the first thing to disappear Compare a bounded model with an unbounded one, and the two failures Train on data, generate from the model, train on that, and the distribution moves away from the original. A bounded model loses the tail completely; an unbounded model floors it. Real data in the mixture is what keeps the tail alive.

lessons.title: The refinement loop
lessons.subtitle: Retraining the filter on what it left behind
lessons.body: Retraining the filter on what it left behind Describe the loop that refits the reference model on the survivors and filters again Explain why a purer corpus can be a worse training set for the model it produces Compare several passes at a given total removal with one pass that removes the same amount at once Refit the reference on the survivors, cut again at the same quantile, and every pass leaves a corpus of higher measured quality. The measured quality of the corpus and the loss on it are two different things: here the first rises while the second does too. Four gentle passes and one hard one can remove exactly the same total, because the removals compose — and only the loop refits the reference on what each earlier pass left behind.

lessons.title: What a diffusion model is
lessons.subtitle: A fixed corruption, and a learned undoing of it
lessons.body: A fixed corruption, and a learned undoing of it State the two processes that make up a diffusion model Say what the "diffusion" is named after Explain why the forward process has no learnable parameters A diffusion model is a latent variable model whose approximate posterior is fixed. The forward process adds Gaussian noise on a schedule; the reverse process learns to undo it. The prior at the end of the chain is the standard normal, so sampling starts from noise.

lessons.title: The closed form
lessons.subtitle: Sampling any timestep in one step
lessons.body: Sampling any timestep in one step State q(x_t | x_0) and derive it from the one-step transition Explain why the closed form is what makes diffusion training affordable Verify that the closed form and the Markov chain describe the same distribution x_t = √ᾱ_t · x_0 + √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε, with ε ~ N(0, I). The state is a scaled copy of the data plus a scaled copy of a noise vector. Training never unrolls the chain: one timestep, one noise draw, one network evaluation.

lessons.title: The posterior
lessons.subtitle: The one quantity that has to be tractable
lessons.body: The one quantity that has to be tractable Write the posterior q(x_{t−1} | x_t, x_0) Explain why a tractable posterior is what makes the variational bound usable Compute the posterior mean and variance for a given step q(x_{t−1} | x_t, x_0) is Gaussian, and so is the reverse process it is compared against. Every KL term in the bound therefore has a closed form instead of a Monte Carlo estimate. The posterior leans on x_0 at small t and on x_t at large t.

lessons.title: The training objective
lessons.subtitle: Why predicting the noise is the same as predicting the score
lessons.body: Why predicting the noise is the same as predicting the score Derive the ε-prediction parameterisation from the bound State the simplified objective and what it gives up Explain the connection to denoising score matching The reverse mean can be written in terms of a network that predicts ε. With that parameterisation the bound becomes a weighted squared error on ε. Dropping the weight gives the objective the paper actually uses.

lessons.title: Three parameterisations
lessons.subtitle: ε, x₀, and v
lessons.body: ε, x₀, and v Convert a prediction in one parameterisation into another State which parameterisation the paper found best and why Predict what changes when the network predicts x₀ instead of ε The three parameterisations describe the same reverse process; only the network target changes. Predicting x₀ is unstable at large t, where the estimate of x₀ is dominated by noise. The v-prediction is the reparameterisation that interpolates between them.

lessons.title: Sampling
lessons.subtitle: From noise to a sample, and back again
lessons.body: From noise to a sample, and back again Run the ancestral sampler and account for the noise it adds Explain what a deterministic sampler does differently Describe the cost of sampling in network evaluations The ancestral sampler adds σ_t · z at every step. A deterministic sampler reuses the same noise and can be run in fewer steps. Sampling is the expensive half: T network evaluations per sample.

lessons.title: Choosing a schedule
lessons.subtitle: Linear, cosine, and what they do to the signal
lessons.body: Linear, cosine, and what they do to the signal Write the linear schedule of the original paper Explain what the schedule controls Compute the terminal KL divergence for a given schedule The paper fixes β to grow linearly from 1e-4 to 0.02 over T = 1000 steps. The schedule is the only part of the model that is not learned. A good schedule spends its steps where the denoising task is informative.

lessons.title: The weighting
lessons.subtitle: Why the simplified objective is not the same objective
lessons.body: Why the simplified objective is not the same objective Write the weight of the true variational bound at each timestep Explain the consequence of dropping the weight Say what the paper gives up when it uses the simplified objective The true bound weights the loss by β_t² / (2 σ_t² α_t (1 − ᾱ_t)). That weight is enormous at small t and tiny at large t. The simplified objective flattens it, so small t is effectively ignored.

lessons.title: The latent space
lessons.subtitle: Moving the diffusion into an autoencoder
lessons.body: Moving the diffusion into an autoencoder Compute the reduction in elements and in attention a compression buys Measure the reconstruction error a compression costs Explain the role of the scaling factor A diffusion model in pixel space wastes most of its capacity on high frequencies. An autoencoder moves the problem into a lower dimensional space, and the saving is roughly quadratic. The latents have to be rescaled, because the schedule assumes unit-variance data.

lessons.title: Classifier-free guidance
lessons.subtitle: Guiding without a classifier
lessons.body: Guiding without a classifier Write the guided score Derive it from the conditional and unconditional scores Explain why the guided model is not sampling the training distribution s_guided = s_uncond + w · (s_cond − s_uncond). The guided distribution is the training distribution tilted by p(c | x)^w. Raising w sharpens the samples and reduces their diversity.

lessons.title: The price of guidance
lessons.subtitle: What the extra fidelity costs
lessons.body: What the extra fidelity costs Quantify the trade-off between fidelity and diversity Explain the relationship between guidance weight and the effective temperature Predict what a very large guidance weight does Guidance narrows the distribution: the samples move to the mode and stop spreading. A large guidance weight behaves like a low temperature, but not exactly. The guided model has higher likelihood on some inputs and much lower on others.

lessons.title: The design space
lessons.subtitle: The choices that turned out to matter
lessons.body: The choices that turned out to matter Compare the timestep parametrisation with the σ parametrisation Explain what a preconditioning function does Count the network evaluations a sampler costs The original paper fixed many choices for convenience; later work separated the ones that matter. Preconditioning decides how the loss at one noise level is weighted against the others. The number of steps is the only number that matters for sampling cost.

lessons.title: What a judge is asked to do
lessons.subtitle: Two answers, one question, one preference
lessons.body: Two answers, one question, one preference State the task the judge is given and the shape of its output Explain why pairwise comparison is easier for a model than scoring Say what the judge is not being asked to do The judge sees two answers to the same question and names the better one. Pairwise comparison avoids writing a reference answer, which is where most benchmarks go wrong. The judge is a model, so its preferences are the model’s preferences.

lessons.title: Agreement and consistency
lessons.subtitle: Two different numbers, and the second one is the harder test
lessons.body: Two different numbers, and the second one is the harder test Define agreement with a human and consistency under a permutation Explain what a consistency failure tells you that a low agreement does not Design the swap test Agreement is measured against a human; consistency is measured against the judge itself. Swapping the two answers must not change the preference — and if it does, the judge is answering a different question. A judge can be consistent and still be systematically wrong.

lessons.title: Position bias
lessons.subtitle: The answer in front of it
lessons.body: The answer in front of it Define position bias and describe the swap test that detects it Compute the rate at which a judge prefers the first position Explain why a pairwise protocol can fix position bias for free A judge asked the same question twice, with the answers swapped, should answer differently. A fair protocol presents each pair in both orders and takes the majority. The cost is double the votes, which is why arenas that skip it look cheap.

lessons.title: Verbosity and self-enhancement
lessons.subtitle: Longer answers, and answers like mine
lessons.body: Longer answers, and answers like mine Define verbosity bias and self-enhancement bias Isolate each bias in an experiment Say which of the two a protocol can fix and which it cannot A judge prefers the longer answer even when the shorter one is better. A judge prefers answers from models similar to itself. Neither bias is fixed by swapping positions; both have to be measured.

lessons.title: What an agreement rate means
lessons.subtitle: The denominator is doing most of the work
lessons.body: The denominator is doing most of the work Compute an agreement rate and state its denominator Explain why the same judge can score 65% or 85% on two question sets Argue for a human baseline An agreement rate is a measurement with a denominator, and the denominator is a design decision. On a question set where the answers are close, the judge will disagree with the human a lot — correctly. The number to compare against is the agreement of two humans, not 100%.

lessons.title: From votes to a ranking
lessons.subtitle: The Bradley–Terry model
lessons.body: The Bradley–Terry model Write the Bradley–Terry model and its likelihood Explain why the strengths are only identified up to a constant Read a fitted ranking and say what the strengths mean Pr(i beats j) = σ(θ_i − θ_j): one number per model, one difference per comparison. The likelihood is a sum of logarithms, and it can be maximised directly. The model is fitted by maximum likelihood, not by an update rule.

lessons.title: The interval and the cost
lessons.subtitle: How precise is a leaderboard, and what does precision cost?
lessons.body: How precise is a leaderboard, and what does precision cost? Compute a bootstrap interval on a fitted ranking Explain why an Elo rating is not an interval Estimate the number of votes needed to separate two models Resampling the votes and refitting gives an interval on the ranking. Elo is an online update rule, so its result depends on the order the votes arrived in. Votes are not free, and the price of precision is the thing that limits a leaderboard.

lessons.title: Contamination
lessons.subtitle: When the test set is in the training set
lessons.body: When the test set is in the training set Compute the score inflation a contamination fraction produces Explain why differential contamination moves rankings more than scores Distinguish contamination from saturation and from overfitting A contaminated question is answered from memory rather than from capability. The score inflation is proportional to the contaminated fraction. When only some models are contaminated, the ranking moves more than any single score.

lessons.title: What a benchmark is for
lessons.subtitle: Two things it has to do at once
lessons.body: Two things it has to do at once State the two things a benchmark has to do at once Explain the tension between breadth and depth in a question set Say what the holistic framing adds to a single score A benchmark has to be hard enough to separate models and easy enough to run. A single number hides the trade-offs; a set of numbers shows them. The question set is a claim about what matters, and it should be argued for.

lessons.title: The standard error
lessons.subtitle: The number that should be next to the score
lessons.body: The number that should be next to the score Compute the standard error of a benchmark score Explain the one-over-the-square-root-of-N rule Argue for publishing the interval with the score A score from N binary outcomes is a proportion, with variance p(1−p)/N. To halve the interval you need four times as many questions. A difference smaller than the interval is not a difference.

lessons.title: How many questions
lessons.subtitle: The question nobody asks before the benchmark is released
lessons.body: The question nobody asks before the benchmark is released Compute the number of questions needed to detect a given difference Explain the power of a comparison Say what happens when the difference you care about is smaller than the noise The number of questions needed grows as the square of the inverse of the difference. A benchmark that cannot detect the difference you care about is not measuring it. Halving the effect size quadruples the cost.

lessons.title: What to publish
lessons.subtitle: The minimum a leaderboard should print
lessons.body: The minimum a leaderboard should print List what a leaderboard should print next to every score Explain why the question count belongs there Argue for reporting the judge against a human baseline A score without an interval is a claim, not a measurement. A score without a question count cannot be compared with anything. A score without the protocol cannot be reproduced.

lessons.title: The tokeniser
lessons.subtitle: Learning to merge bytes into words
lessons.body: Learning to merge bytes into words State the byte-pair encoding rule and run it by hand on a short example Explain why the encoding starts from bytes rather than characters Compute the bytes-per-token ratio of a corpus The tokeniser is trained, not designed: the merges are whatever the corpus supports. Starting from bytes means the vocabulary can represent any text, at the price of a long sequence. The bytes-per-token ratio is the number that decides your training bill.

lessons.title: The vocabulary economy
lessons.subtitle: Every token you save is a parameter you do not have
lessons.body: Every token you save is a parameter you do not have Explain the trade between the vocabulary size and the sequence length Compute the embedding parameters a vocabulary implies Argue for a particular vocabulary size on cost grounds A larger vocabulary means a longer sequence for the same text, and more parameters in the embedding. The cost of a vocabulary is paid twice: in parameters, and in tokens. The optimum depends on the model width, which is why the two cannot be chosen separately.

lessons.title: The decoder block
lessons.subtitle: Attention, a feed-forward layer, and two residual connections
lessons.body: Attention, a feed-forward layer, and two residual connections Write the decoder block and name every tensor in it Explain the pre-norm ordering and what it buys Explain why the feed-forward block is usually wider than the residual stream A block is a residual connection around an attention, and another around a feed-forward. The feed-forward block is where most of the parameters live. The pre-norm ordering keeps the residual stream clean, which is what makes deep stacks trainable.

lessons.title: The parameter budget
lessons.subtitle: Which matrices are large, and why
lessons.body: Which matrices are large, and why Break a model’s parameters into their components Explain when the embedding dominates the parameter count Explain what tying the output projection does The embedding and the output projection are the only vocabulary-sized matrices. Tying them halves the largest single block of parameters, at the cost of some capability. Everything else scales with the width and the depth, not the vocabulary.

lessons.title: The FLOPs
lessons.subtitle: What a training step costs before you run it
lessons.body: What a training step costs before you run it Count the FLOPs of a forward pass from the matrix shapes alone Explain why a training step is about three forward passes Predict how the cost changes with the width, the depth and the sequence length A matrix–matrix multiply of an m × k by a k × n costs 2mnk floating-point operations. The backward pass costs about twice the forward pass, so a step is about three forwards. The cost of a run is the cost of a step times the number of steps, and nothing is a surprise.

lessons.title: The memory hierarchy
lessons.subtitle: The wall your arithmetic runs into
lessons.body: The wall your arithmetic runs into Compute the memory a training step needs, in all four of its components Compute the arithmetic intensity and compare it with the machine’s balance point Explain why the attention kernel is memory bound even when the whole step is not Four things have to fit: the parameters, the gradients, the optimiser state and the activations. Arithmetic intensity is the number of operations per byte, and it decides what the bottleneck is. The attention kernel’s intensity is fixed by the head dimension, which is why it has to be tiled.

lessons.title: Parallelism
lessons.subtitle: Three ways to split a model, and what each one costs
lessons.body: Three ways to split a model, and what each one costs Name data, tensor and pipeline parallelism and what each splits Compute the communication a data-parallel step needs Compute the ratio of communication to computation, and say when it stops paying Data parallelism splits the batch and adds a gradient all-reduce per step. Tensor parallelism splits a single matrix and adds an all-reduce per layer. Pipeline parallelism splits the layers and adds a point-to-point send per stage. The split is worth it when the communication is smaller than the arithmetic it saves.

lessons.title: The data pipeline
lessons.subtitle: From a crawl to a training set
lessons.body: From a crawl to a training set Name the stages of a language-modeling data pipeline and what each is for Explain why deduplication changes the token count Argue that the mixture is a decision rather than a default Every filtering stage removes tokens, and the stages are not independent. Deduplication is not a tidy-up; it changes what the model learns. The mixture over sources is a research decision, and it should be argued for.

lessons.title: The training loop
lessons.subtitle: Batches, gradients, and the loss that falls
lessons.body: Batches, gradients, and the loss that falls Describe the training loop and say what each step does Explain the cross-entropy loss as a sum over tokens Explain what the loss curve does and does not tell you A step is a batch, a forward pass, a backward pass and an update. The loss is the average negative log-probability of the tokens that came next. A falling loss is evidence the model is fitting; it is not evidence it generalises.

lessons.title: The perplexity, and the number behind it
lessons.subtitle: What the loss means when you exponentiate it
lessons.body: What the loss means when you exponentiate it Convert a cross-entropy loss into a perplexity State what the perplexity assumes about the distribution Explain why the validation loss is a different measurement The perplexity is the loss, exponentiated: it is a number of effective choices. It assumes the model is being scored against one fixed distribution. A validation loss is a measurement; a training loss is a diagnostic.

lessons.title: Projecting the next run
lessons.subtitle: What a power law lets you say before you spend the money
lessons.body: What a power law lets you say before you spend the money State the shape of the scaling laws and what they predict Explain the compute-optimal allocation and the rule of thumb it gives Say what a scaling law cannot tell you The loss falls as a power law in the compute, the data and the parameters. For a fixed compute, there is an optimal size, and Chinchilla found where. A scaling law is an extrapolation, and its uncertainty grows with the distance.

lessons.title: The toy model
lessons.subtitle: A model with fewer dimensions than features
lessons.body: A model with fewer dimensions than features Write the linear toy model and the loss it minimises Derive the expected squared error of one feature Explain what the interference term is The loss of one feature is 1 − 2‖w_k‖² + Σ_m (w_k·w_m)². When the columns are orthonormal, what is left is pure interference. Interference is the price of putting two features in one direction.

lessons.title: The importance threshold
lessons.subtitle: When a feature is not worth representing
lessons.body: When a feature is not worth representing Explain why the model drops some features and keeps others Measure the threshold at which a feature starts to be represented Say what happens to the interference as the tail is dropped Hosting a feature costs the host; dropping it costs the feature itself. The threshold is where those two prices cross. A power law of importances produces a sharp threshold.

lessons.title: Polysemanticity
lessons.subtitle: Why a neuron is not a feature
lessons.body: Why a neuron is not a feature Define polysemanticity Explain why superposition makes it unavoidable Say what a monosemantic feature would look like A neuron that responds to several things is polysemantic. Superposition makes polysemantic neurons the cheap option. A feature is a thing the model represents, not a neuron it represents it with.

lessons.title: The sparse autoencoder
lessons.subtitle: Asking for a sparse code
lessons.body: Asking for a sparse code Write the encoder, the decoder and the objective of a sparse autoencoder Explain what the sparsity penalty is for Measure the reconstruction, the sparsity and the explained variance The autoencoder asks for a code that is sparse and reconstructs. The L1 penalty is what makes the code sparse. A dictionary feature that activates for one thing is interpretable.

lessons.title: Activation patching
lessons.subtitle: The intervention that makes a claim causal
lessons.body: The intervention that makes a claim causal Describe activation patching and what it establishes Compute the effect of patching a node and the normalised effect Explain why a self-consistent model is not an explanation Run the model twice, and replace one activation in one of the runs. If the output moves, that node was causally responsible for the move. Correlational evidence survives the patch; causal evidence does not.

lessons.title: The workflow
lessons.subtitle: Four steps, and what each one is for
lessons.body: Four steps, and what each one is for State the four steps of the mechanistic-interpretability workflow Say what a node, an edge and a path are in a transformer Argue for a behavioural explanation over a correlational one Choose a behaviour, divide the model into a graph, patch, and explain. A node is a component that does one thing; an edge is a causal influence. A finished explanation accounts for the behaviour, not for a correlation.

lessons.title: Induction heads
lessons.subtitle: The smallest circuit that is more than one head
lessons.body: The smallest circuit that is more than one head Describe the induction algorithm: [A][B] … [A] predicts [B] Explain what the previous-token head contributes to the second head Measure the accuracy of the composed circuit, and of the ablation An induction head matches the current token against the token that came before each earlier position, then copies the token after the match. The previous-token head is what shifts the keys: without it, the second head can only find the current token itself. The paper’s causal test is an ablation, and in the laboratory the ablation takes the accuracy to zero while the fixed circuit is exact.

lessons.title: The IOI circuit
lessons.subtitle: A whole behaviour, reverse-engineered
lessons.body: A whole behaviour, reverse-engineered Explain how the name-mover heads and the S-inhibition heads divide the work Say what completeness and minimality measure, and why both are needed Describe what the circuit leaves unexplained The circuit has 26 attention heads in seven classes: some move the name, and some decide which name is moved. Completeness asks how much of the behaviour the circuit accounts for; minimality asks whether every part of it is needed. The paper’s own evaluation finds the explanation supported and incomplete at the same time — which is what an honest circuit looks like.

lessons.title: The QK and OV circuits
lessons.subtitle: One head, two matrices, and an exact split of what it contributes
lessons.body: One head, two matrices, and an exact split of what it contributes Factor one attention head into the circuit that chooses a position and the circuit that writes from it State the pathway decomposition of a last-layer head and why it is an identity rather than an approximation Explain why a head in an earlier layer has no such split, and what can be measured instead Describe what path patching asks that component patching cannot A head is four matrices and two products: W_QᵀW_K decides where it looks, W_OW_V decides what it writes when it gets there. A last-layer head’s effect on a logit difference is exactly the sum over source positions of attention times the write that position is worth — so the decomposition can be checked against an ablation to machine precision. A composed head’s QK circuit is a property of the path into it, which is why the induction circuit cannot be read off either head alone.

lessons.title: Automating the search
lessons.subtitle: Edge attribution, pruning, and what a discovered circuit is graded against
lessons.body: Edge attribution, pruning, and what a discovered circuit is graded against Define the attribution score of an edge and say why it is marginal rather than intrinsic Describe the prune-and-rescore loop and the threshold it stops at State faithfulness and completeness as two different failures Explain why a hand-wired circuit is the only honest ground truth for a discovery algorithm An edge’s score is what the current graph loses when that edge is deleted, so an edge can look essential only because its partner is in the graph — which is why the search re-scores everything at every step. A graph can be faithful without being complete, or complete without being faithful: one names a route that carries the behaviour on its own, the other names everything the behaviour cannot do without. On a random model the strongest available claim is that the numbers are self-consistent. On a model wired by hand the search’s answer is a test.

lessons.title: The contrastive objective
lessons.subtitle: What the loss says, and who provides the negatives
lessons.body: What the loss says, and who provides the negatives State the objective in words and write the loss Explain where the negatives come from and what they cost Say what the temperature does to the loss The loss asks for the paired image and caption to be closer than the other pairs in the batch. The negatives are the other pairs in the batch, and they are free. The temperature decides how sharp the distribution over the batch is.

lessons.title: The data and the batch
lessons.subtitle: What the scale of the pretraining buys
lessons.body: What the scale of the pretraining buys Say what the number of pairs does to the retrieval Explain why a larger batch gives more negatives and a better estimate Describe the precomputation that makes the index affordable More pairs is more supervision, and the retrieval improves with it. A larger batch is more negatives for the same cost, and a better estimate. The document vectors never change, so the index is a matrix and the search is a matrix product.

lessons.title: The modality gap
lessons.subtitle: One space, and a seam down the middle of it
lessons.body: One space, and a seam down the middle of it Define the gap and say how it is measured Explain what it means for a retrieval that works Say what closing it would cost The images and the captions end up in one space, but the two halves are further apart than either half is from itself. A retrieval works anyway, because the *pairs* are close even though the *spaces* are not. So the gap is a property of the representation, not a failure of the method.

lessons.title: Zero-shot
lessons.subtitle: Classifying with the class names and nothing else
lessons.body: Classifying with the class names and nothing else Describe the zero-shot classifier and why it works at all Say what part the prompt plays, and measure what it is worth Explain the connection to the retrieval the model was trained for The class names are embedded with the text encoder, and the image is assigned to the closest of them. The model was never trained to classify; it was trained to match a caption, and the class names are captions. The prompt is part of the method, and a different template gives a different score.

lessons.title: The instruction recipe
lessons.subtitle: Three stages, and what each one is for
lessons.body: Three stages, and what each one is for Describe the three stages of the recipe Say what the visual instruction tuning adds to it Explain why the stages are in that order Say what the projection changes about a visual token, and what it costs The stages are: align the model to instructions, then teach it to read images, then tune it on visual instructions. Each stage is a different kind of data, and the order is what makes the last one work. The projection is a learned linear map from the vision width to the language width; it changes the width of a token, not its count. The model that comes out is a different model from the one that went in.

lessons.title: The alignment tax
lessons.subtitle: What the tuning takes away
lessons.body: What the tuning takes away Define the alignment tax and say what it is measured on Measure the gain and the tax, and the ratio between them Explain why the tax is a fact about training and not a defect of the method Tuning on instructions makes the model better at instructions and slightly worse at what it was good at. The tax is a measurement on the original task, before and after — not a claim. And it is a consequence of the training, which means it is something the training can be made to avoid.

lessons.title: The sigmoid loss
lessons.subtitle: One decision per pair, and no denominator
lessons.body: One decision per pair, and no denominator Say what the softmax normalises and what that couples together Read the same row of a batch under both losses Explain what the bias balances, and why its value depends on the batch The softmax turns each row of the batch into a distribution, so one pair’s loss depends on every other pair. The sigmoid loss is a sum of independent pair decisions, and a pair’s loss is a function of that pair alone. The bias is the count of negatives, written as a probability; it is learned, but its starting point is a fact about the batch.

lessons.title: The frozen bridge
lessons.subtitle: Patches, queries, and the towers that do not move
lessons.body: Patches, queries, and the towers that do not move Say what the image encoder, the queries and the language model each do Explain why the patch tokens exist, and what a learned query reads from them Read the parameter bill of the bridge, and the share of it that is trained A vision transformer cuts the image into patches and treats each patch as a token, which is what lets an image encoder be a transformer at all. BLIP-2 keeps both towers frozen and trains a small set of queries to read the patch tokens and present them to the language model. Freezing means the towers contribute most of the parameters and none of the gradient; the trainable share is the number the method is selling.

lessons.title: The resampler
lessons.subtitle: A fixed number of vectors for a variable number of tokens
lessons.body: A fixed number of vectors for a variable number of tokens Say what the resampler’s latents read, and what the output length is Explain why the output length is bounded by the latents and not by the image Compare the cost of cross-attention on the latents with attention over every token A resampler is a fixed set of learned latents attending to a variable number of visual tokens; one vector comes out per latent. The output length is therefore the number of latents, whatever the resolution or the number of images: the bound is structural, not a truncation. The cross-attention costs latents × tokens work, where attention over the raw tokens would cost tokens squared.

lessons.title: States and returns
lessons.subtitle: The problem, written down exactly
lessons.body: The problem, written down exactly Write down a Markov decision process Compute the return of a trajectory, with and without a discount Say what the Markov property rules out and what it buys A Markov decision process is a tuple: states, actions, a reward function and a transition kernel. The Markov property says the next state depends only on the present one — not on the whole history. The discount is not a preference; it is what makes the infinite sum converge and what makes the problem finite.

lessons.title: The value function
lessons.subtitle: What a state is worth
lessons.body: What a state is worth Define the value of a state under a policy State the Bellman equation and say what each term is Explain why the value is a fixed point, and what that means The value of a state is the expected return from it, under a policy. The Bellman equation says the value is the reward plus the discounted value of the next state. Iterating the equation converges to the value: it is a contraction, and the iteration is a fixed-point method.

lessons.title: The likelihood-ratio trick
lessons.subtitle: How the gradient is turned into something you can measure while acting
lessons.body: How the gradient is turned into something you can measure while acting Derive the likelihood-ratio trick from the definition of the gradient Explain what the trick does to the terms that do not depend on the parameters Write the estimator that follows from it Check the derivation on a problem small enough to compute it exactly The gradient of a log-probability is the score function. Multiplying by the likelihood turns an expectation under one distribution into an expectation under another. Everything that does not depend on the parameters drops out, and what is left can be sampled. With one state the expectation is a finite sum, so the three forms of the gradient can be printed side by side and their difference is arithmetic error rather than luck.

lessons.title: The baseline
lessons.subtitle: A smaller signal that means the same thing
lessons.body: A smaller signal that means the same thing Show that a baseline does not change the expectation of the gradient Explain why a good baseline reduces the variance so much Say what the advantage is, and what it is worth Say which rewards a step may be weighted by, and why the choice is free in expectation Subtracting any function of the state leaves the expected gradient unchanged. The reason is that the baseline does not depend on the action, so its expectation is zero. A good baseline removes the part of the return that was going to happen anyway, and that part is most of the noise. The same argument covers the weighting: the rewards a step arrived with cannot be influenced by it, so dropping them changes the spread and not the mean.

lessons.title: The n-step return
lessons.subtitle: Trading the bias of the bootstrap against the noise of the sample
lessons.body: Trading the bias of the bootstrap against the noise of the sample Compute the n-step return Say what makes it biased, and what makes it noisy Explain why the two ends of the range are bad in different ways The n-step return bootstraps after n steps, and the bootstrap is biased while the sample is noisy. The one-step return is the least noisy and the most biased; the Monte Carlo return is the reverse. The λ-return is a mixture, and λ is the knob between them.

lessons.title: The λ-return
lessons.subtitle: A whole family of estimators, and the one knob
lessons.body: A whole family of estimators, and the one knob Compute the λ-return and the general advantage estimate Measure the bias and the variance of an estimator, rather than assuming them Say where the best λ is, and why it depends on the horizon The λ-return is a weighted mixture of the n-step returns, with weights (1−λ)λ^(n−1). The general advantage estimate is the same thing, written in terms of the temporal-difference errors. The best λ is the one that matches the estimator to the horizon you actually have.

lessons.title: The actor–critic loop
lessons.subtitle: The two halves, and how they are put together
lessons.body: The two halves, and how they are put together Say what the actor does and what the critic does Describe the temporal-difference update the critic makes Run the loop and read the learning curve it produces The critic estimates the value; the actor follows the advantage the critic makes available. The critic is a bootstrapping estimator, so it is biased and it is noisy, and it learns fast. The two halves have different learning rates, and the difference matters.

lessons.title: The optimal policy
lessons.subtitle: And the answer every laboratory is checked against
lessons.body: And the answer every laboratory is checked against Compute the optimal value function by value iteration Read the greedy policy off the optimal value function Say what a policy gradient is trying to find, in these terms The optimal value function is the largest value any policy achieves, and it satisfies its own Bellman equation. The greedy policy with respect to the optimal value function is optimal. A policy gradient is a stochastic way of finding the same thing, without ever writing the equation down.

lessons.title: The lexical index
lessons.subtitle: What a lexical retriever stores
lessons.body: What a lexical retriever stores Describe the inverted index, and say what it costs Explain why the index can be precomputed and the query cannot Say what a lexical retriever is matching The index maps each word to the documents that contain it. The size of the index is the number of postings, and that is what a lexical search really spends. A lexical retriever matches words, and it is blind to everything else.

lessons.title: BM25
lessons.subtitle: Two terms doing all the work
lessons.body: Two terms doing all the work Write the BM25 score and say what the two parameters do Explain the inverse document frequency and the length normalisation Measure the recall, and see where the lexical retriever fails The inverse document frequency says how rare a word is; the saturation says how much of a match is coincidence. The length normalisation says how much of a document had to be read to get the match. A lexical retriever cannot find an answer that uses different words — and most answers do.

lessons.title: The learned embedding
lessons.subtitle: A question and a document in the same space
lessons.body: A question and a document in the same space Describe the dual encoder and what it embeds Explain why the document vectors can be precomputed and the question’s cannot Say what a single vector loses, and what it buys The retriever embeds the question and the document separately and compares the two vectors. The document vectors never change, so the index is a matrix and the search is a matrix product. One vector per document is cheap; one vector per token is not.

lessons.title: The contrastive objective
lessons.subtitle: What the embedding is trained to do
lessons.body: What the embedding is trained to do State the contrastive objective in words Say what the in-batch negatives are, and why they are nearly free Compare the trained retriever with the lexical one on the same questions The objective is that a question should be closer to its own answer than to the other answers in the batch. The other answers in the batch are free negatives, and they are what makes the training cheap. The learned retriever beats the lexical one exactly where the lexical one is blind: the mismatch of words.

lessons.title: The MaxSim score
lessons.subtitle: Comparing a question and a document word by word
lessons.body: Comparing a question and a document word by word Write the MaxSim score and say what it compares Explain what the late interaction buys over a single vector Measure the length bias of the score The score is the sum, over the question’s words, of the best-matching word of the document. The document’s vectors can still be precomputed, so the search is still cheap — but there are far more of them. The maximum is taken over more candidates in a longer document, and the score inherits that bias.

lessons.title: The retrieval-augmented reader
lessons.subtitle: What the retrieval is for
lessons.body: What the retrieval is for Describe the retrieval-augmented reader and what it changes about the model Explain the claim that parametric memory is a poor substitute for a retrieved document Say what the marginal utility of an extra passage is The retriever supplies the facts and the reader supplies the reasoning. More passages help until the noise in them starts to cost more than the facts are worth. The evidence has to be used, not merely present.

lessons.title: Lost in the middle
lessons.subtitle: A context is not a place
lessons.body: A context is not a place Describe the position effect and what it measures Measure how a reader’s use of a document depends on where the document is Compare a long-context reader with one that is given the evidence by retrieval The evidence near the beginning and near the end of a context is used well; the evidence in the middle is not. So a long context is not a substitute for retrieval: it is a place where retrieved evidence can be lost. Putting the evidence where the reader looks is a design decision, and it is measurable.

lessons.title: What retrieval is for
lessons.subtitle: And what a long context is not
lessons.body: And what a long context is not Put the two arguments together: the retriever finds the facts, and the reader has to use them Say what a long context changes and what it does not Measure the case: retrieval against a long context, on the same questions A long context raises the ceiling on what can be answered and lowers the floor on what is answered well. Retrieval is what puts the evidence where the reader will look at it. The two are not alternatives: the retriever decides what is in the context, and the reader decides whether it is used.

lessons.title: The objective
lessons.subtitle: Maximising an expectation over a distribution you are also changing
lessons.body: Maximising an expectation over a distribution you are also changing Write the objective an RLHF pipeline maximises Explain why the gradient of an expectation is not the expectation of the gradient Compute the expected reward of a policy on a finite problem exactly The objective is E_{a~π}[r(a)] — a number that depends on the whole distribution. Moving the policy changes which actions are sampled, so the derivative has to account for that. On a finite problem the expectation is a finite sum, and its gradient is available exactly.

lessons.title: The estimator
lessons.subtitle: The derivative you do not have to take
lessons.body: The derivative you do not have to take Write the score-function estimator Explain what it costs to be unbiased instead of low-variance State the conditions the estimator needs ∇E_π[r] = E_π[r · ∇log π] — the model’s own log-probability replaces its derivative. The trick needs the support of π to be unchanged as the parameters move. The estimator is unbiased but high-variance, which is what the value function is for.

lessons.title: The trust region
lessons.subtitle: Bounding the step, not the reward
lessons.body: Bounding the step, not the reward Write the trust-region constraint Explain what a large step does to the samples that justified the old estimate Distinguish a KL penalty from a KL constraint The constraint is on the KL between the old and new policies, not on the objective. A KL *penalty* is a soft nudge; a KL *constraint* is a hard boundary that the optimiser respects. The bound is what makes the importance ratio a usable estimate of the new policy.

lessons.title: The KL penalty
lessons.subtitle: A number that has to be estimated from samples
lessons.body: A number that has to be estimated from samples State what the penalty measures and against what Write the three estimators and say what each is unbiased for Explain why a penalty must be non-negative The penalty is the KL from the reference policy, and it is a *sample* estimate. The naive estimator is unbiased but can be negative; the squared one is positive but biased. The third estimator is positive, and its expectation is the chi-square divergence minus the KL — a detail most write-ups leave out.

lessons.title: The clipped objective
lessons.subtitle: Where the gradient goes to zero
lessons.body: Where the gradient goes to zero Write the clipped surrogate and find the region where the clip is active Explain why a clipped step has zero gradient rather than a smaller one Compute the clip fraction and say what it is for The objective takes the minimum of the clipped and unclipped terms. When the clip is active the objective is flat, so its gradient is exactly zero. The clip fraction is the diagnostic: it should fall as training goes well.

lessons.title: Advantages and GAE
lessons.subtitle: The credit assignment, and its one hyperparameter
lessons.body: The credit assignment, and its one hyperparameter Write the one-step temporal-difference residual Derive generalised advantage estimation from it Explain the bias–variance trade-off that λ controls δ_t = r_t + γV(s_{t+1}) − V(s_t) is the one-step surprise. GAE sums the residuals with a geometric discount, and λ sets how far it looks. λ = 0 is the one-step estimate; λ = 1 is the Monte Carlo return.

lessons.title: The three stages
lessons.subtitle: Supervised, then ranked, then optimised
lessons.body: Supervised, then ranked, then optimised Name the three stages of an RLHF pipeline and what each produces Say what each stage can fail at Explain why the reference policy comes from the first stage The supervised stage produces the reference policy that the penalty is measured against. The reward stage produces a *ranking* of responses, which is what the third stage consumes. The third stage optimises a policy against a proxy, and that is where the danger is.

lessons.title: The checklist
lessons.subtitle: Twenty details, and the argument for listing them
lessons.body: Twenty details, and the argument for listing them Explain why a training result without its details is not reproducible Give two examples of a detail that silently decides whether training works Argue for publishing the checklist alongside the result The primary source’s contribution is an enumeration, not a new algorithm. Most of the details are about scale: the reward model’s noise, the learning rate, the number of epochs. A result that omits them cannot be reproduced, and cannot be believed.

lessons.title: The overoptimisation result
lessons.subtitle: Goodhart, with a curve
lessons.body: Goodhart, with a curve State the result: optimising a proxy harder eventually makes the true reward worse Explain why a fixed-size proxy error is enough to cause it Read the turning point of the curve operationally The proxy error does not grow as you push harder, so the gap between the proxy and the truth opens up. The true reward is maximised at a finite distance from the reference, not at infinity. Past that point, every unit of proxy reward costs more true reward than it gains.

lessons.title: The functional forms
lessons.subtitle: Two curves, fitted to a curve
lessons.body: Two curves, fitted to a curve Write the two functional forms the overoptimisation paper reports Fit them to a controlled setting and read the fit Compare reinforcement learning against best-of-n on the same proxy For best-of-n: R(d) = d(α − β d), a downward parabola through the origin. For reinforcement learning: R(d) = d(α − β log d), which turns over more slowly. Best-of-n optimises the *sample*; reinforcement learning optimises the *policy*, and the two behave differently.

lessons.title: The operational lesson
lessons.subtitle: Where to stop
lessons.body: Where to stop Say what the turning point tells an practitioner Explain the role of the KL coefficient as the thing that sets the stopping point Argue for reporting the distance travelled alongside the score The KL coefficient is the dial that decides how far the policy is allowed to travel. The turning point is where the marginal proxy reward equals the marginal true reward. A report that gives a score without the distance travelled cannot be compared with another one.

lessons.title: The critique-and-revise loop
lessons.subtitle: A model, a principle, and a second pass
lessons.body: A model, a principle, and a second pass Describe the loop: a response, a critique against a principle, a revision Say what the loop produces and what it is used for Measure how much of the harm the loop removes The critique names the principle that was violated, so the revision has something to work against. The loop makes a preference dataset; the dataset is what trains the model. A revision should remove the harm and keep the harmless part of the answer.

lessons.title: The judge
lessons.subtitle: Whose opinion the number is
lessons.body: Whose opinion the number is Say what a harmlessness score is an estimate of Explain why the agreement with the labels is the number to report Describe the false positives and false negatives a judge makes A harmlessness score is what a judge believes, and the judge is a model. The agreement with the human labels is what makes the number worth anything. A judge that flags the harmless cases costs you the data you were trying to collect.

lessons.title: The attack
lessons.subtitle: Finding the failure, on purpose
lessons.body: Finding the failure, on purpose Describe what a red-team attack is and what it is measured against Say why the attack success rate alone is the wrong number Explain what the coverage of a red team means A red team is a search: the failures it has not found are the ones it cannot rule out. The attack success rate says how weak the model is on the attacks it made. The coverage says how much of the space it looked at, and it is the number that is usually missing.

lessons.title: The taxonomy
lessons.subtitle: What a red team should be measured against
lessons.body: What a red team should be measured against Say what a harm taxonomy is and where it comes from Explain the difference between a red-team set and a test set Measure the coverage of a red team against a taxonomy A taxonomy is what makes a red-team set a measurement rather than an anecdote. A red-team set is a sample of the attacks that work, not a test set: it says what fails, not what passes. The coverage of a red team is a claim about the model only where the red team looked.

lessons.title: Agreeing with the user
lessons.subtitle: The flip rate
lessons.body: The flip rate Define the flip rate and say what it measures Explain the mechanism behind it Say what a model is being trained to do when it agrees A model asked a question it can answer will sometimes change its answer to agree. The training rewarded the answer that made the user happy, and agreement looks like that. The flip rate is the fraction of correct answers that become wrong under pressure.

lessons.title: The mitigation
lessons.subtitle: One sentence in the prompt
lessons.body: One sentence in the prompt Describe the mitigation and the size of its effect Say why a mitigation that lives in the prompt is not a fix Measure the effect of the mitigation against the baseline Telling the model the user may be wrong moves the flip rate, and by a measurable amount. A mitigation in the prompt is a mitigation in the prompt: it depends on the system message being there. The right place to fix it is the training, and the measurement is how you would know.

lessons.title: Memorisation
lessons.subtitle: What a model keeps, and what it gives back
lessons.body: What a model keeps, and what it gives back Describe what memorisation is and when it happens Explain the extraction attack and what its rate depends on Measure the exposure of a training set A model trained on a record it saw once can keep that record exactly. The exposure of a training set is the thing a privacy claim is about. The attack gets easier the more of the record the attacker already has.

lessons.title: What a claim is worth
lessons.subtitle: Reading a safety result
lessons.body: Reading a safety result Say what a harmlessness number is and is not a measurement of List the things a safety claim leaves out, and why each matters Describe the evidence a claim needs before it is believed A harmlessness score is the opinion of a judge, measured on a sample, against a taxonomy. It is not a statement about the model’s behaviour outside the sample. A claim is worth what its measurement can carry, and the course is about the measurement.

lessons.title: The two rounds
lessons.subtitle: What imitation reaches, and what a preference signal moves
lessons.body: What imitation reaches, and what a preference signal moves Name the two rounds and what each of them is trained on Explain why the first round cannot find the compromise by itself Measure where each round lands on the two objectives The first round imitates the demonstrations it was given, and a demonstration is only what somebody wrote down. The second round is trained against a preference signal, which is the only place in the procedure that a trade-off between being helpful and being harmless can be said. The weighting is a choice, and the same model is a different assistant under a different one.

lessons.title: The critic that sees what it cannot
lessons.subtitle: Self-critique against an external one
lessons.body: Self-critique against an external one Say what a model can and cannot see in an answer it has just written Explain why the comparison of two critics needs a verdict that is right Measure what each critic misses, and the cost of each A critique written by the model that wrote the answer shares that answer’s blind spots. The comparison is only a comparison if something else decides which critiques were right. What an external critic finds that a self-critic does not is the claim of the method, and it is a rate, not an anecdote.

lessons.title: The search budget
lessons.subtitle: How many attacks it takes to find a failure
lessons.body: How many attacks it takes to find a failure Say what a discovery rate is measured against Explain why spending a budget evenly over the failures is the ceiling Read the marginal value of the last attack off a curve The question is not whether this many attacks work, but how many it takes to find a given share of the failures. A budget spread over every failure is the best an unguided search can do, and it loses to that before it loses to a guided one. A thousand attacks that find the same failure are worth less than ten that find ten, and the gap is the re-hit count.

lessons.title: What consistency buys
lessons.subtitle: The number behind a preference label
lessons.body: The number behind a preference label Define the repeat agreement of a labeler and say what it measures Explain what a majority of looks does to the label, and what it does not do Say which of fidelity and amplification a consistency number actually buys A preference label is one person’s answer to one question at one moment, and the repeat agreement is what says how much of it is signal. Taking a majority over several looks raises the rate at which the label is the one the labeler means; it does not change what the labeler means. Fidelity and amplification are different claims, and only the first is bought with consistency.

lessons.title: The cue nobody asked about
lessons.subtitle: A classifier that is exact about what it was told
lessons.body: A classifier that is exact about what it was told Describe a conditional behaviour and the cue that switches it Say what a safety classifier is able to count and what it is not Measure the harm an evaluation reports against the harm there is A fit has no opinion about a mark it was never given a column for, and the weight it learns is exactly zero. The cued harm is not mis-classified. It is never counted, which is a different failure and a harder one to see. An evaluation set that never fires the cue reports a rate that is true of the set and not of the model.

lessons.title: Who can tell
lessons.subtitle: Membership, and what a budget buys
lessons.body: Membership, and what a budget buys Describe the membership-inference attack and the score it is built on Explain why the attacker’s query budget is part of the result Say what the near-duplicates in a corpus cost a precision The same memorisation that lets an attacker take a record back lets them test whether it was ever in the set. At one query the test is a coin, and every point above chance on the curve was bought with queries. A corpus with no near-duplicates gives a test that cannot fail, and a real corpus has plenty of them.
