lessons.title: What a power law says
lessons.subtitle: And why the exponent is the number everyone quotes
lessons.body: And why the exponent is the number everyone quotes State the form of a scaling law and the three quantities in it Convert an exponent into the factor a doubling of the data buys Distinguish a power law in the loss from a power law in the error A power law says that the loss falls as L ∝ N^(−α) — a constant factor for every doubling. The exponent is the whole of the practical content: a doubling buys a factor 2^(−α). The error, not the loss, is the quantity that scales cleanly near the floor.

lessons.title: How the exponent is measured
lessons.subtitle: Log–log space, and the range the fit depends on
lessons.body: Log–log space, and the range the fit depends on Fit a power law by least squares in log–log space Read the R² of the fit and say what it does and does not certify Show that the fitted exponent changes with the range of the data The fit is a straight line in log–log space, and ordinary least squares is the right tool for it. A high R² says the points are close to a line; it does not say the line will keep holding. A fitted exponent is an average over a range, and quoting it without the range is quoting half a result.

lessons.title: The compute budget
lessons.subtitle: The constraint that makes the question a question
lessons.body: The constraint that makes the question a question Write the cost of a training run as a function of the parameters and the tokens Explain why a budget turns "how big" into "big in what way" Measure the loss along a fixed budget The cost of a run is the number of parameters times the number of tokens, times a constant. Under a fixed budget, more parameters means fewer tokens, and the loss of each is measured against the other. A budget is a statement about what cannot be had, and it is the only reason the allocation is a decision.

lessons.title: The compute-optimal allocation
lessons.subtitle: Where the two terms of the loss balance
lessons.body: Where the two terms of the loss balance Write the two-variable loss surface and fit it Derive the condition that balances the two terms at the optimum Compute the allocation and the tokens-per-parameter ratio at a given budget The surface is E + A·N^(−α) + B·D^(−β): an irreducible term and two powers. At the optimum the two terms balance in a fixed ratio, and that fixes the allocation. The tokens-per-parameter ratio at the optimum is a consequence, not a setting.

lessons.title: The crossover between size and data
lessons.subtitle: Kaplan’s question: at what budget does the bigger model start to pay?
lessons.body: Kaplan’s question: at what budget does the bigger model start to pay? State what a crossover point is, and which two losses are being set equal Derive the product at which two given capacities are equally good Explain why the crossover moves when the pair of capacities gets wider At a fixed budget the two candidates get D = P/N rows each, so the comparison is one equation in one unknown. Below the crossover the small model trained on more data wins; above it the large model trained on less wins. The crossover is a property of the fitted surface, and it is only as good as the grid of runs the surface was fitted on.

lessons.title: The IsoFLOP curves and the frontier
lessons.subtitle: A U at each budget, and the power law its bottoms obey
lessons.body: A U at each budget, and the power law its bottoms obey Write the loss along a fixed budget and find its minimum in closed form State the exponent of the frontier and derive it from the two single-variable exponents Compare the analytic optimum with the one found by numeric search Every point of an IsoFLOP curve costs the same, so the curve is a statement about choice rather than about spend. The bottom is where the two marginal losses balance, and that balance gives N* and D* without a search. The bottoms across budgets fall as C^(−αβ/(α+β)) — the frontier is a consequence of the surface, not a new measurement.

lessons.title: The twenty-tokens rule, rederived
lessons.subtitle: What the ratio at the optimum is, and what it is not
lessons.body: What the ratio at the optimum is, and what it is not Derive the tokens-per-parameter ratio the optimum chooses for itself Measure the exponent of that ratio against the budget on a fitted surface Say which property of the surface makes the rule a constant, and which makes it a trend The ratio is a consequence: D*/N* has an exponent (α−β)/(α+β) and is flat only when the two exponents agree. The predicted allocation exponents and the measured ones are two instruments on one fact, and the screen prints both. A rule quoted without the budget it was measured at is a number that will not travel.

lessons.title: When the pool binds
lessons.subtitle: The budget at which the data runs out, and what happens past it
lessons.body: The budget at which the data runs out, and what happens past it Compute the budget at which the optimal allocation asks for the whole corpus Explain why the frontier and the achievable loss come apart past that budget Read the price of the constraint off the optimum at a binding budget The frontier says how much data the optimum wants; a corpus is a finite number of rows, and that is where the two stories diverge. Beyond the binding budget, extra compute buys repeats rather than data, and the loss falls more slowly than the law says. The size of the pool is a variable, and the same budget is unconstrained in one corpus and bound in another.

lessons.title: The three phases of a repeated run
lessons.subtitle: Warmup, plateau, and the turn upward
lessons.body: Warmup, plateau, and the turn upward Name the three phases and say what each one is a fact about Explain why the gap between the repeated and the fresh run is exactly zero at the first epoch Read the decay phase off a held-out curve rather than off a training curve At one epoch the two runs have read the same rows, so they are the same run — the warmup is arithmetic, not behaviour. The plateau is the pool’s empirical optimum in sight and the fresh data still buying real improvements. The decay is the repeated run walking towards a fit to the noise in its own pool, and it shows on held-out data first.

lessons.title: How many epochs before repetition dominates
lessons.subtitle: The dominance epoch, and the fraction that defines it
lessons.body: The dominance epoch, and the fraction that defines it Define the dominance epoch and say what it is measured against Show that the epoch you report depends on the fraction you chose Compare the measured dominance epoch with the one the paper’s constant predicts Repetition dominates when the next epoch is worth so little that the compute would have been better spent on new rows. The criterion is a fraction of the fresh run’s gain, and the table of fractions is the honest version of a single number. The closed form says half a fresh epoch at R★·ln 2 passes; the measured curve is allowed to disagree, and the screen prints the disagreement.

lessons.title: The turn upward, and the early-stopping epoch
lessons.subtitle: The pool gets easier while the model gets worse
lessons.body: The pool gets easier while the model gets worse Explain why the loss on the pool keeps falling after the held-out loss has turned upward Read the best epoch off a held-out curve, and say what the run loses by passing it State why a single restart is not a curve The pool has its own optimum, which is a fit to the noise planted in the pool; past the shared optimum the two come apart. The third phase is not a change in the optimiser. It is the same descent aimed at a target that is not the task. The compute already spent is not a reason to keep going, and the loss that is visibly falling is not the loss being bought.

lessons.title: When the data runs out
lessons.subtitle: Repeats, and what they are worth
lessons.body: Repeats, and what they are worth Define the number of repeats and the effective number of unique tokens Write the loss of a learner trained on repeated data Show that repetition does not change the model a ridge estimator finds E repeats of U unique rows is E·U rows of training and U rows of information. The ridge normal equations are homogeneous in the data, so the solution is unchanged by repetition. What repetition buys is the illusion of progress: the same model, at a higher price.

lessons.title: The price of repetition
lessons.subtitle: Fresh rows against the same rows again
lessons.body: Fresh rows against the same rows again Compare a repeated run with a fresh run of the same length on the same held-out set Measure how the gap grows with the number of repeats State the practical rule the measurement supports Fresh rows keep improving the estimate; repeated rows stop improving it immediately. The gap between the two is the price of repetition, and it is paid in compute. The rule that falls out is about *unique* tokens, not about tokens.

lessons.title: The effective-data law
lessons.subtitle: D′ = U·(1 + R★·(1 − e^(−R/R★))), evaluated rather than quoted
lessons.body: D′ = U·(1 + R★·(1 − e^(−R/R★))), evaluated rather than quoted Write the law and say what each of the three quantities in it is Compute the ceiling a pool is ever worth, and the epoch at which a pass is worth half a fresh one Name the thing the law has no term for, and say which screen measures it The first pass is worth exactly itself; every later pass is worth e^(−R/R★) of a fresh epoch, which is a decay with no knee in it. R★ is the whole of the law’s content: it sets the ceiling U·(1 + R★) and the epoch at which the marginal pass halves. The law saturates and a real run turns upward, so the ceiling bounds the law’s optimism rather than the run’s achievement.

lessons.title: The percolation threshold
lessons.subtitle: When the rows going are the rows nothing else can replace
lessons.body: When the rows going are the rows nothing else can replace State the percolation argument for a threshold keep fraction Read a threshold, a best fraction and a cliff edge off one pruning curve Explain why the threshold is a property of the metric’s queue rather than of the pool alone Volume laws say a smaller corpus is a worse corpus in a fixed way; percolation says that past some fraction the loss goes faster, because what is being removed stops being redundant. The rare rows carry the tail directions, and a direction covered by three rows stops existing when two of them are cut. Rank the same pool four ways and the same event happens at four different fractions, because each ranking loses the rare rows when its own queue reaches them.

lessons.title: Four metrics on one pool
lessons.subtitle: Oracle, strong, weak, random — and what each ranking costs
lessons.body: Oracle, strong, weak, random — and what each ranking costs Rank four pruning metrics at matched volume and read each one’s own threshold Explain the difference between a comparison at matched volume and one at matched compute Say which of the four metrics a practitioner can actually compute, and what that costs The oracle ranks rows by the information they truly carry and nobody has it; it is the ceiling the computable metrics are scored against rather than a fifth option. A strong metric has to be fitted over the whole pool before it can score a row, so its win on volume has to survive a baseline handed the same number of extra rows. The paper’s ordering — strong beats weak, weak beats random, each with its own cliff — is a claim, and the table is the test of it on this pool with this seed.

lessons.title: Predicting the cliff before it happens
lessons.subtitle: m rare rows per direction, and the survival of a queue with error in it
lessons.body: m rare rows per direction, and the survival of a queue with error in it Compute the threshold the structure of a pool predicts, with no free parameter Compare the predicted fraction with the measured one on the same pool Say what the prediction does as the metric’s error grows past the information spread The prediction is a survival calculation: how many rare rows are expected to outrank the cut at each keep fraction, against the number the tail directions need. At zero error the answer is the share of the pool that ranks above the rarest rare row — a property of the pool, not of the loss. Past the information spread a rare row survives a cut exactly as often as a bulk row does, the predicted threshold goes to one, and there is nothing left to prune.

lessons.title: What emergence looks like
lessons.subtitle: A score that is zero, and then is not
lessons.body: A score that is zero, and then is not Describe the shape of an emergent curve and what makes it striking Read an emergent curve and say what it does not establish about the model Compute the same capability under a second, continuous metric The curve is flat, then steep, and the steep part is where the attention goes. A flat region is not a model that cannot do the task; it is a metric that cannot see it. The same model, scored differently, can look smooth.

lessons.title: Reproducing the artefact
lessons.subtitle: One sweep, two readings, and the gap between them
lessons.body: One sweep, two readings, and the gap between them Define the reporting floor and read an onset off it Find the widest gap between the per-token accuracy and the whole-sequence score on one sweep Explain why the location of a cliff is a fact about the floor as much as about the model The onset is the first point above a chosen floor, so the claimed discovery moves when the floor moves — and the floor is a defensible choice, which is not the same as a forced one. The gap is widest in the middle of the climb: that is where “the model cannot do this” and “the model gets most of the tokens right” are both true, and only one of them is about the metric. A cliff interval needs two onsets, and the underlying accuracy never has one because it never stops rising.

lessons.title: What causes the cliff
lessons.subtitle: A threshold in the metric, on a smooth capability
lessons.body: A threshold in the metric, on a smooth capability Derive the whole-sequence score as a power of the per-token accuracy Show that the sharper the metric, the sharper the apparent transition Show that moving the metric’s threshold moves the cliff A whole-sequence score is the per-token accuracy raised to the length of the sequence. The longer the sequence, the steeper the apparent transition — and nothing about the model changed. The cliff is in the metric; the capability underneath it is smooth all the way.

lessons.title: Three eras and one straight line
lessons.subtitle: The reported slope, the reported doubling, and the reported range
lessons.body: The reported slope, the reported doubling, and the reported range Convert a slope in orders of magnitude a year into a doubling time, and back Say why the reported range of an era and the reported slope of it disagree Name which numbers on the screen are quoted from the paper rather than computed A slope and a doubling time are one statement in two units, and the conversion is exact: twelve times log₁₀2 divided by the months. A range is an envelope — the two most extreme runs — and a slope is a trend through a scattered middle, so reading the first as the second is how a headline growth rate is made. The eras are placed by the analyst: one boundary is a date in the middle of a year rather than a bin, because the event it marks is a date.

lessons.title: A break in the trend, and what it costs to claim one
lessons.subtitle: Every split, both sides fitted, and a penalty of two log n
lessons.body: Every split, both sides fitted, and a penalty of two log n Describe the split search and the penalty a detected break has to pay Explain why a series that is exactly straight must not report a change of slope Say why a break is a claim about the future rather than a description of the past The search tries every split, fits both sides, and keeps the smallest residual sum of squares only once the split has paid for its two extra parameters. Requiring the two slopes to differ is what stops floating-point noise from being read as a discovery. One trend over a broken series is not wrong so much as averaged: it reports the middle of two rates and predicts neither.

lessons.title: What a trend buys, and the year it became buyable
lessons.subtitle: Inverting the frontier, dividing by a wall-clock, reading a series
lessons.body: Inverting the frontier, dividing by a wall-clock, reading a series Name the three steps from a loss target to a year, and what each one assumes Explain why the factor between the budget’s units and FLOP/s moves every date and no shape Read the flag that says whether an answer was interpolated inside the series or projected outside it The frontier inverted gives the budget a loss costs, the budget over the run’s hours gives the rate, and the series read at the rate gives the year. The surface’s budget is in the units of its own runs, so the bridge to FLOP/s is an assumption; halving it changes every date by a predictable amount and changes nothing else. A target at or below the fitted floor cannot be bought at any price, and reporting that is the answer rather than a failure to produce one.

lessons.title: The matrix you never build
lessons.subtitle: Where the memory goes in a long context
lessons.body: Where the memory goes in a long context Write the naive attention and say what it materialises Compute the size of the score matrix and the traffic it causes Distinguish the memory a training run needs from the memory a forward pass needs The score matrix is N by N, and it dwarfs everything else at a long context. It is written once and read once, and then it is thrown away. The training run is worse than the forward pass, because the backward pass needs the matrix kept.

lessons.title: The running softmax
lessons.subtitle: An exact answer, computed without the matrix
lessons.body: An exact answer, computed without the matrix Describe the tiling: which block is resident, and which is streamed past Derive the running maximum, the running sum and the rescaling between them Check that the tiled algorithm and the naive one agree The softmax of a row can be accumulated as a running maximum and a running sum. When the maximum moves, the accumulator is rescaled — and that rescaling is what keeps it exact. The answer is identical; only the memory and the traffic differ.

lessons.title: Decoding is memory-bound
lessons.subtitle: The arithmetic intensity of one token
lessons.body: The arithmetic intensity of one token Compute the bytes the key and value cache holds for a given context Compute the arithmetic intensity of a decode step Explain why the intensity rises with the batch size and then stops A decode step is a matrix-vector product: two operations per byte of weights. The weights are read once for the batch; the cache is read once per sequence. So the batch amortises the weights and nothing else — and the intensity saturates.

lessons.title: The page table
lessons.subtitle: Memory you can actually hand out
lessons.body: Memory you can actually hand out Explain why a contiguous allocation wastes memory on the padding Describe the paged allocation and what it wastes instead Compute the waste of both for a set of sequence lengths A straightforward implementation gives every sequence a buffer as long as the longest one. Paging replaces the buffer with fixed-size blocks that can live anywhere. The waste becomes a fraction of a block per sequence rather than a fraction of the batch.

lessons.title: The router
lessons.subtitle: Which experts see this token
lessons.body: Which experts see this token Describe the top-k router and the probabilities it assigns Define the load of an expert and the probability mass it receives Explain what happens when the two disagree The router sends each token to the few experts with the highest scores. The load is what the experts actually got; the probability is what the router wanted. When they disagree, some experts are trained more than others — and the ones trained less are worse.

lessons.title: The auxiliary loss
lessons.subtitle: Paying a little to keep the experts equal
lessons.body: Paying a little to keep the experts equal Compute the auxiliary loss from the load and the probability Show that it grows when the router is biased Measure the overflow that a capacity factor allows The auxiliary loss is the number of tokens times the sum of the products of the two fractions. It is smallest when the load and the probability agree, and it pushes the router there. The capacity factor is the other half of the bargain: a hard limit, and the tokens it drops.

lessons.title: Proposing and checking
lessons.subtitle: The rule, and what it guarantees
lessons.body: The rule, and what it guarantees State the acceptance rule and compute the rate it implies Show that the procedure produces the target model’s own distribution Explain why the corrected token is drawn from the excess A drafted token is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)). The expected acceptance is one minus the total variation between the two distributions. The two terms of the output distribution — the accepted and the corrected — add up to the target’s.

lessons.title: When speculation pays
lessons.subtitle: The trade, and its terms
lessons.body: The trade, and its terms Compute the tokens produced per target step from the acceptance rate Compute the speed-up, and say what it depends on Explain why a closer draft model is worth more than a longer one The speed-up is the tokens per step, divided by the cost of the drafting. A draft that is close to the target is worth more than a long run of a bad one. The output is unchanged: the method buys time, not a different answer.
